title: Only living/formed faith justifies; Stapleton, Bellarmine, Vasquez, Becanus
source_text: XLII. Praeterea fatentur fidem mortuam atque otiosam hominem non justificare, illamque nihil omnino prodesse ad justitiam & salutem: ac proinde nos sola fide viva, & quae per dilectionem operetur, justificari. Ita Thomas Stapletonus Anglus in Academia Duacensi Professor, asserit pluribus in locis, fidem sine charitate & opere obedientiae mortuam esse, id est, ut ipse exponit, ad salutem & justitiam prorsus ineptam, vanam, & inutilem. Sicuti videre est libro de Justificatione, cap. 2. & cap. 13. Et Prolegomenis in librum quintum, ex Apostolo docet, fidem ad justitiam consequendam nihil valere, nisi operetur per dilectionem. Similiter Bellarminus lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 14. multis argumentis probat fidem quae separata est a spe & dilectione, ac proinde quae viva non est, justificare non posse. Quibus accedit Vasquez, tom. 2. in primam secundae disput. 110. cap. 7. num. 54. ubi observat fidem, quam Concilium Tridentinum docet habere rationem radicis & fundamenti in nostra justificatione, esse illam quae movet & excitat affectum: fidem autem quae affectum non movet, neque ex se actuosa est, ut alliciat voluntatem ad bonum, rationem istam radicis & fundamenti non habere. Ideoque merito Becanus Jesuita, in Summa Theologiae Scholasticae, tom. 2. tract. 4. cap. 2. num. 7. Catholicis suis tribuit, quod communi consensu docent solam fidem formatam, quo nomine Schola Romana designat illam quae cum charitate juncta est, justificare. Catholici, inquit, docent fidem non justificare, nisi sit formata charitate. Item, Catholici docent, cum Augustino, fidem posse informem existere, non tamen nisi formatam justificare.
pass_a_gloss: Further, they confess that dead and idle faith does not justify a man, and that it profits nothing at all toward righteousness and salvation: and therefore that we are justified by living faith alone, and that which works through love. Thus Thomas Stapleton, Englishman, Professor in the Academy of Douai, asserts in many places that faith without charity and the work of obedience is dead—that is, as he himself explains, utterly unfit for salvation and righteousness, vain, and useless. As may be seen in his book On Justification, chapters 2 and 13. And in the Prolegomena to the fifth book, from the Apostle he teaches that faith is of no avail for obtaining righteousness unless it works through love. Likewise Bellarmine, book 1 On Justification, chapter 14, proves by many arguments that faith which is separated from hope and love, and therefore which is not living, cannot justify. To whom Vasquez adds, volume 2 on the Prima Secundae, disput. 110, chapter 7, number 54, where he observes that the faith which the Council of Trent teaches to have the character of root and foundation in our justification is that which moves and stirs affection; but faith which does not move affection, and is not of itself active so as to draw the will to the good, does not have that character of root and foundation. And therefore Becanus the Jesuit rightly attributes to his Catholics, in the Summa of Scholastic Theology, volume 2, tract 4, chapter 2, number 7, that by common consent they teach that only formed faith—by which name the Roman School designates that which is joined with charity—justifies. Catholics, he says, teach that faith does not justify unless it is formed by charity. Likewise, Catholics teach with Augustine that faith can exist unformed, yet only formed faith justifies.
pass_b_english: Rome agrees: only living faith that works through love justifies; dead faith profits nothing.
Stapleton, Bellarmine, Vasquez, Becanus: formed faith (with charity) alone justifies.
